(NHC) Hurricane Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, is expected to bring damaging winds, heavy rain and potentially life-threatening storm surge to the northern Gulf Coast when it makes landfall late Friday or early Saturday. The governors of Florida, Alabama and Georgia have declared states of emergency, along with several Mississippi counties. Thousands of National Guard soldiers are being deployed. According to the National Hurricane Center , Isaias is a Category 2 storm with sustained winds of 110 mph. "Isaias is likely to become a major hurricane this morning. Slight weakening is expected before landfall, but it is expected to remain a dangerous hurricane." Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The storm could make landfall near the Alabama-Florida state line, though its exact path remains uncertain. Heavy rain and flooding could extend as far north as Tennessee and North Carolina through the weekend. Mandatory evacuation orders have been issued for parts of Florida's Walton, Escambia, Okaloosa and Franklin counties. Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey also ordered nonresidents to evacuate Gulf Shores, Orange Beach and Dauphin Island. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis urged residents to prepare emergency supplies and "execute your hurricane plan." "Residents should take this storm seriously and evacuate," Okaloosa County officials warned. Follow live updates on Hurricane Isaias below. Flash and urban flooding is likely across the region Fri, Oct 09, 2026 11:55 AM UTC Jasmine Andersson Hurricane Isaias mapped An infographic shows how Hurricane Isaias is set to intensify as it reaches the U.S. Gulf Coast. (Anadolu via Getty Images) This graphic based on NOAA data shows the potential track of Hurricane Isaias as it moves north from the Gulf of Mexico. The image shows Isaias is forecast to strengthen into a major hurricane, with winds above 110 mph, before weakening slightly as it nears the Gulf Coast. It is then forecast to weaken to a tropical storm over Alabama and to a tropical depression as it moves northeast through Tennessee and Kentucky toward West Virginia. Fri, Oct 09, 2026 11:42 AM UTC Tom Parfitt FEMA facing Isaias test following staffing cuts Hurricane Isaias could test FEMA's ability to respond to disasters following significant staffing reductions, according to the Guardian . More than 4,300 FEMA employees left the agency in fiscal year 2025, representing about 17% of its workforce, according to a Government Accountability Office report. The departures included dozens of senior officials, raising concerns about the loss of experienced personnel. Chris Currie, a director at the Government Accountability Office, told the Guardian, "It's not whether FEMA is going to respond. They're going to respond. It's more about the depth." Disaster survivors advocate Ginny Goldman described the hurricane as FEMA's "biggest test" since the staffing reductions. A FEMA spokesperson said, "Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin's leadership, the safety of the American people is DHS's top priority. FEMA incident management assistance teams are deploying to Alabama and Florida, and FEMA personnel are embedded in state emergency operations centers. FEMA is also prepositioning emergency supplies at Maxwell Air Force Base in Montgomery, Ala., to supplement state resources if requested."
